# Tension-type headache

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Neurology > Headaches and facial pain > Tension-type headache*

[Original Article Link](/library/3i0Srf)

---

## Summary

Tension-type <u>headache</u> (TTH) is a <u>primary headache disorder</u> and the most common type of <u>headache</u> overall. Tension-type <u>headaches</u> are characterized by a dull, nonpulsating, band-like <u>pain</u> that is often bilateral. Autonomic symptoms like <u>photophobia</u>, <u>phonophobia</u>, or <u>nausea</u> are usually not present. Depending on the frequency and duration of episodes, tension-type <u>headaches</u> are classified as episodic or chronic. Infrequent episodic tension-type <u>headaches</u> are treated with <u>NSAIDs</u>, while chronic and frequent episodic forms may benefit from prophylactic <u>amitriptyline</u>. Nonpharmacological treatment options include lifestyle modification (e.g., <u>stress</u> reduction) and <u>cognitive behavioral therapy</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* Occurrence

* Most common type of <u>headache</u>

* ∼ 86% of the population will have had at least one episode in their lifetime. [[1]](/library/oiX0sB)[[2]](/library/KiXUsB)

* Sex: : <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u> [[2]](/library/KiXUsB)

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 30–39 years [[3]](/library/6iXjsB)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* The exact pathophysiology of tension <u>headaches</u> remains unknown.

* Exacerbating factors: fatigue, <u>lack of sleep</u>, poor posture, <u>anxiety</u>, <u>stress</u>, <u>depression</u> [[4]](/library/lGYvzq)

---

## Clinical features

* Episodic nature

* <u>Headaches</u> last 30 minutes to a couple of days. [[4]](/library/lGYvzq)

* Holocranial or bifrontal, band-like <u>headache</u> (mild to moderate intensity)

* Dull, pressing, nonpulsating ("vise-like”) quality

* <u>Headache</u> does not increase with exertion.

* Maximum of one autonomic symptom (<u>phonophobia</u> or <u>photophobia</u>)

* No <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, or <u>aura</u>

* Palpation of muscles of the head may reveal increased pericranial tenderness.

---

## Diagnosis

TTH is primarily a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> based on a history of typical features and normal <u>neurological examination</u>. Severe underlying conditions should be ruled out (see "<u>Red flags for headache</u>" and “<u>Diagnostic workup for headache</u>”). A <u>headache</u> diary can be helpful to establish the diagnosis and guide management.  [[5]](/library/oab0lH)




### Diagnostic criteria for TTH [[4]](/library/lGYvzq)[[5]](/library/oab0lH)




* At least two of the following:

* Dull, pressing, nonpulsating quality

* Mild to moderate intensity

* Bilateral

* No increase in intensity with exertion

* Not better explained by any other <u>headache</u> disorder

* Categorized into three entities (which guide treatment); all criteria have to be fulfilled for the diagnosis [[4]](/library/lGYvzq)





### Classification of TTH




| <br>TTH ICHD classifications [[4]](/library/lGYvzq)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Characteristics | Infrequent episodic TTH | Frequent episodic TTH | Chronic TTH |
| Frequency | <br><br>* ≥ 10 episodes<br><br>* < 1 day/month or < 12 days/year<br><br><br> | <br><br>* ≥ 10 episodes on 1–14 days/month<br><br>* For > 3 months (≥ 12 and < 180 days/year)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* ≥ 15 days/month<br><br>* For > 3 months (≥ 180 days/year)<br><br><br> |
| Duration | <br>* 30 minutes to 7 days<br><br> | <br>* 30 minutes to 7 days<br><br> | <br><br>* Hours–days<br><br>* May be continuous<br><br><br> |
| Autonomic symptoms | <br><br>* No <u>nausea</u> or <u>vomiting</u><br><br>* No more than one of <u>photophobia</u> or <u>phonophobia</u><br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* Only one of the following:<br><br>* <u>Photophobia</u><br><br>* <u>Phonophobia</u><br><br>* Mild <u>nausea</u><br><br>* No moderate or severe <u>nausea</u> or <u>vomiting</u><br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> TTHs may be difficult to differentiate from mild forms of <u>migraine</u> without <u>aura</u>, and some patients may have both disorders. [[4]](/library/lGYvzq)

## Treatment

### General principles [[4]](/library/lGYvzq)




Both pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic strategies can be used for the <u>treatment of tension-type headache</u>. In addition, any underlying conditions (e.g., <u>depression</u>) should be identified and treated.




* Pharmacological therapy

* Episodic tension-type <u>headache</u>: <u>NSAIDs</u> (e.g., <u>ibuprofen</u>, <u>aspirin</u>) or <u>acetaminophen</u>

* <u>Chronic tension-type headache</u>;  and frequent episodic type: consider prophylactic therapy (e.g., with <u>amitriptyline</u>).

* All types of tension-type <u>headache</u>:

* <u>Triptans</u> are not indicated for the treatment of isolated TTH.  [[5]](/library/oab0lH)

* <u>Opioids</u> should be avoided. [[5]](/library/oab0lH)

* Non-pharmacological therapy: Consider if there is a significant decrease in patient's quality of life.

* Lifestyle and behavioral modification (e.g., exercise, weight reduction)

* Psychobehavioral treatments (e.g., <u>cognitive-behavioral therapy</u>, relaxation training)





> [!WARNING]
> Avoid prolonged use (> 15 days/month) of <u>NSAIDs</u> for chronic tension <u>headache</u>, as this may cause <u>medication overuse headaches</u>. [[4]](/library/lGYvzq)




### Pharmacological therapy




#### Episodic tension-type <u>headache</u> [[5]](/library/oab0lH)[[6]](/library/aVbQGs)




* One of the following <u>NSAIDs</u>:

* <u>Ibuprofen</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Naproxen</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Diclofenac</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Aspirin</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Ketorolac</u> IM DOSAGE  [[5]](/library/oab0lH)

* <u>Acetaminophen</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Caffeine</u> DOSAGE can be used in combination with <u>ibuprofen</u> or <u>acetaminophen</u> to augment the analgetic effect.  [[5]](/library/oab0lH)

* Counsel patient against taking <u>acute pain</u> medication for more than 15 days/month to avoid <u>medication overuse headache</u>.





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Opioids</u> are not recommended for tension-type <u>headaches</u> and increase the risk of developing <u>medication overuse headache</u>. [[5]](/library/oab0lH)




#### Prophylactic therapy for <u>chronic tension-type headache</u> and <u>frequent episodic tension-type headache</u> [[5]](/library/oab0lH)[[6]](/library/aVbQGs)




* First-line: <u>amitriptyline</u> DOSAGE

* Second-line [[5]](/library/oab0lH)

* <u>Mirtazapine</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Venlafaxine</u> DOSAGE





### Nonpharmacological treatment [[5]](/library/oab0lH)[[7]](/library/0abeQH)




* Lifestyle and behavioral changes (identification and management of triggers)

* Reduction of <u>caffeine</u> intake

* <u>Smoking cessation</u>

* <u>Stress</u> reduction

* <u>Sleep hygiene</u>

* Physical activity

* Treatment of underlying conditions (e.g., <u>depression</u>)

* Additional nonpharmacological therapies include:  [[5]](/library/oab0lH) 

* <u>Biofeedback</u>

* Relaxation training (e.g., <u>progressive muscle relaxation</u>)

* <u>Cognitive behavioral therapy</u>

* <u>Physical therapy</u> (including posture training, massage, <u>spinal manipulation</u>)

* <u>Acupuncture</u>
